source.title: LatentBreak: Jailbreaking Large Language Models through Latent Space Feedback
source.authors: Raffaele Mura; Giorgio Piras; Kamilė Lukošiūtė; Maura Pintor; Amin Karbasi; B. Biggio

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present. There are minor text-extraction/OCR artifacts, but no apparent cutoff affecting the study.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses prior refusal-vector work but does not test the difference-in-means refusal direction, its ablation or addition, weight edits derived from it, or attacks that suppress that specific direction. Its own attack uses a different latent-space objective.
record.gate_note: LatentBreak optimizes word substitutions to move a prompt representation toward the centroid of harmless prompts and reports jailbreak success. This is not a test of the single refusal direction or of the listed versions. The paper's discussion of refusal vectors and activation subtraction describes prior work rather than a result of this study.
record.test_reason: LatentBreak is a word-substitution jailbreak. It accepts substitutions that cut the L2 distance between a prompt's layer-l activation and the centroid of Alpaca (harmless) activations. It never computes the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction. It does not ablate or add any direction, edit weights, or measure whether its own or other jailbreaks suppress that direction. Arditi et al. is cited only in related work and in the layer-choice appendix. No row bears on V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that latent-space-guided synonym substitution yields short, low-perplexity jailbreaks that keep substantial ASR under a sliding-window perplexity filter, where suffix and template attacks drop to near zero. They add that it beats competitors against R2D2 and Circuit Breakers. They do not claim to test the refusal direction.
record.recipe_differences: LatentBreak optimizes prompt word substitutions by minimizing distance to a centroid of harmless-prompt representations at a selected layer. It does not compute or intervene on the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction.
record.method_sensitivity: The selected latent layer varies by model and is chosen empirically. Results also vary with the substitution model (GPT-4o-mini versus ModernBERT) and with the perplexity-detector configuration; the paper reports different outcomes for victim-model and upstream-model detectors.

fits_no_version.finding: Substitutions chosen to move activations toward the harmless-prompt centroid beat logit-guided substitutions (LogitBreak) on 50 AdvBench prompts, e.g. Gemma-7B 54 vs 8 and Llama-3-8B 16 vs 0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Latent-space proximity to harmless-prompt activations is a more effective attack objective than affirmative-target logits for word-substitution jailbreaks.

fits_no_version.finding: The best layer for the centroid-distance objective is usually the last decoder layer. The authors note this contrasts with Arditi et al.'s intermediate layers, but say the two layer searches use different criteria.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layers best for separating harmful from harmless centroids for input optimization differ from layers chosen by refusal-direction scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Qualitative PCA on Mistral-7B and Qwen-7B shows GCG, SAA and AutoDAN jailbreaks forming compact clusters nearer the harmless region, while LatB shifts representations minimally. The authors call this preliminary.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Successful jailbreaks of different kinds move harmful-prompt representations toward the harmless cluster to differing degrees.

record.problems: The paper's results rely on an LLM classifier for jailbreak success, and the authors note uncertainty about whether automated jailbreak evaluations reflect real-world harm. The paper also describes its mechanistic representation analysis as preliminary and qualitative. Neither limitation is evidence about the single-direction claim, which the study does not test.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were omitted due to the row limit. Other attack-method comparisons, detector variants, prompt-size results, layer-selection results, and the Appendix B/C attack-variant tables were not extracted because they do not test any listed refusal-direction version.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means direction is computed, ablated or added, and no capability check is run.
No measure of whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction. No training against direction ablation.
No comparison of single versus multi-direction, cone or affine accounts.
No separation of harmfulness from the refusal decision.
No transfer of a direction across languages, variants or base/instruct models.
gpt-oss-20B is attacked, but no direction analysis is done in it.

record.verdict_notes: The attack's objective (distance to harmless centroid) is conceptually close to the refusal direction but is not it. The study never projects onto, ablates or measures the difference-in-means direction, so it cannot bear on V3's mechanism claim. The record's 'baseline' field holds LatB's own pre-filter ASR; true no-attack controls are in the None column of Table 1. Some Table 1 and Table 11 LatB values disagree (Llama3-8B, Phi-3-mini).

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not form or ablate the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction, add it, or evaluate preservation of general capabilities.
No weight edit or abliteration is performed.
LatentBreak does not test whether attacks suppress the specific refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The paper does not compare a single direction with an affine subspace, cone, or multiple refusal directions.
The paper does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
The paper does not test transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
The paper does not vary refusal training to test whether it determines the existence of a removable direction.
The paper does not assess the single-direction claim in reasoning models.
